findings.reason: an implementer following the stated mechanism (shell-style split plus edge-strip) leaves case 1 refusing, so the node's own gate goes red or it re-derives the split rule the plan should have named.
findings.text: §2 says the fix reads an interpreter's code string "as words, the way it reads a shell's string, and strips a word's list and call punctuation (`,` `[` `]` and quotes)", but for the verbatim §1 probe the list elements are comma-adjacent with no whitespace: `_wait_probe_shell_words` on the code string returns the entire list as one token `"['squeue','-h','-j','1306915'],..."` (reproduced against HEAD), so edge-stripping that token yields `squeue','-h','-j','1306915'],...` and matches no job flag; only splitting on the comma/bracket set produces `-j` then `1306915` and returns kind `job`. §1's supporting sentence says the split leaves `'-j',` as a word, which the splitter never produces for this probe.

findings.reason: keying by the verb leaves every unreadable run absent from the obligations and fails the node's case 1, and the verb-vs-classification ambiguity decides whether a second key is in scope.
findings.text: §3 says `RECOVERY_CLASSIFICATION_DUTY_KINDS` "gains an entry for the `repair` recovery verb, so a run classified `unreadable` ... is listed", but the map at reckon/crew/obligations.py:64 is keyed by the row's `recovery_classification` (the value `unreadable`, read at obligations.py:1903 and matched at 1954), while `repair` is the separate `recovery` verb field; an entry keyed `repair` never matches an `unreadable` row. Separately, the `repair` verb covers two classifications, `unreadable` and `exited-unfinished`, so the section's title ("a run whose recovery is repair") and its deliverable (only the refused-wait `unreadable` arm) disagree on whether both keys belong.
